game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I think I got this for free some months ago and now got to play it. It ran rather fine on an Ubuntu 18.04 lapttop with Nouveau drivers, game has native Linux support. 
You play as a worker for a surveillance program, sorting through the web and accessing peoples devices, looking for clues about terrorists. I cant really compare the game to anything, maybe it is similar to a graphical novel to some extent, as you have limited choices, but you do have to use your head, even if the game pretty much always at least tells you where to look for clues.  
It was almost an initimate experience to look into the character life, their private chats and calls. I feel like they could have added a bit more "useless" webpages, to make the game more authentic, but it is obvious that they tried  to give their characters depth, which is where the game shines. 
As the name of the game tells us, to some extent it is obviously a political/ethical game, even if done rather abstract (you work for "the nation", and pretty much everyone you investigate did something wrong). 
One thing I really appreciated, was that they show what can happen if systems like this make mistakes, which is something I feel like is not discussed enough as a counterargument to surveillance, besides the obvious ethical ones.  Overall the the game is an interesting experience, but not comparable to games like "Spec Ops -  The Line", where you really have to get your hands dirty, which lessens the impression of consequences of the players actions in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Highly recommended.
When I saw this game for the first time, I thought "hey, the idea is awesome, but is it done with love and care ? since it doesn't support my native language, will I be able to understand what happens in game ?"... Then I gave it a try and loved what I found.
Let's be crystal clear: if you are looking for fast-paced action, this game is not for you at all. But if you like to dig, read, think, deduce, then it's totally for you. All you need is to be able to understand written english. You are never rushed, you can take all the time you need before making a choice.
Basically, the game makes you in command of a powerful system able to read mails, hack phones and computers, access many databases. You are the one who can dive into this huge pool of datas, and you choose what interesting parts to transmit to police people (or to keep for yourself !). A bombing just occured and your goal is to find the culprits and make sure no other killings occur. You have a bunch of suspects and you'll have to find their secrets, relationships, motives, and finally find who is manipulating who...
I had a really great time with this game, maybe you are the next one :)
Edit: nomination event wants me to update a review. I will never say too much how I love Orwell !

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Well, it takes a a while to finish this game, and I dunno how to describe it properly. This game is quite easy if you a just a clicker but not a reader, you might finish it within 2 hours, maybe even less. But if you are looking for stories, you might find it pretty good (and more difficult). I am not an anti-utopia fan, nor a orwell fan, the narration is the only thing attracts me. 

[spoiler]The story began in a metroplis called Bonton. There was a bomb attack and you got to find out the anwser, who, and why. You were the investigator, using the program called ORWELL. As your investigation went deeper, there would be more bomb attacks. You caught the wrong guy, she was a suspect but not the attacker. "so who is?" you asked. The curiosity drove you moving further and further, until everything was too late and you had to make your own desicion. You couldn't go back, you had to find out the truth. You had to thing what is right for the Nation, for the citizens. 
[/spoiler]

This game reminds me of an old game once I played called Hacknet, the difference is, this is more like in microsoft style, while the hacenet is in linux style. xd

This game is different from Her Story, too. Tho they are all good at narration. I always have no idea what should I search in Her Story, and I gotta watch the videos over and over again to find out the connections (tho there is a guildbook and yes I know it). You can read in your speed in Orwell, and everything there is readable even if it is a phone call and you don't have to listen at all. It's friendly to me, cuz I cannot hear clearly when it goes fast (I mean the normal speed). 

It has multiple endings, so you can totally play it more than once to collect or whatever you want. (It seems there are not too much collect elements except those portraits... xd)

The UI is pretty adorable to me, very sci-fi, white and blue, kinda like assassin's creed style. 

This is a puzzle game, you gotta use your logic and reason to figure what do do, which info is needed while which is not. Especially in the fifth chapter and you gotta figure out the anwser within 20 uploads and no hints, you gotta consider it carefully. 

When I was a kid I always play detective games, took some adventures, went to some ruins with my mates, searching some old newespapers or books and read, like there were some secrets in them, or fought the mosters in our imagination. Now I am an investigator and the Nation's fate is hanging in the balance, cannot be more excited. 

For a lot people it might hard to understand, non-native English speaker like me. A lot Chinese people said that they need a translation, they even joked that this is a comprehension exam. But I find it much easier than I thought. There are plenty of daily words, not too much unfamiliar ones. You can open your browser when you play it, so you can google anytime. So it is still friendly to the non-native English speakers anyway. The translation would be a huge work, I never expect that.

p.s. The profile in this game can be also paired with the new profile in Orwell: Ignorance is Strength, if you bought both.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I believe Fellow Traveller Games is very interested in making people switch to Tails with giving away their published "Linux basics" game Hacknet for free (multiple times even!) first, and now give away this game too to fuel your paranoia and use some of that know-how to make you try and hide.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.
There is no way to change the font neither through options nor through config files, forum searches gave nothing in regards to that either, so be mindful of that.

Firstly this is a visual novel, so no super exciting and engaging gameplay is to be found, but honestly that may be for the better in these spying games.

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Running on PopOS Linux (and this game has a linux client)... crashed on activating the first achievement.

Which is about the time I was ready to walk away from the game anyway.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell's design does a good job at disguising the fact that it is pretty much basically just a very fancy visual novel. This isn't really a huge deal because it's still pretty entertaining, but there's not a whole lot of game in this game. Your advisor tells you pretty much everything you need to do and then like a cog in a machine, you just do it. 
There's a sorta hamfisted political message that it presents well and fairly subtly initally, but then fumbles towards the end of the game. It goes well with the story.
The one issue that I found to be pretty damaging with Orwell is that for such a story driven game, I didn't feel any emotions towards the characters. They're pretty average archetypes that are awkwardly written, as if one talented writer wrote the framework for the game and another less talented writer wrote the dialogue. The only real connection I formed was with the advisor character, which was just a shell for nearly 90% of the game, as a way to inject tutorial into the story without breaking immersion. 

I hope you like reading, because it's about 6 hours worh of reading.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is only getting more relevant in the years since it’s release given it’s subject matter of government surveillance. It is kind of a visual novel puzzle game where you navigate different platforms finding bits of info that you can tag to the database which in turn can find you more info. As you go on you start to unravel a story of who was behind the bombings. The bits of info are highlighted so you can’t miss them and you also don’t always have to tag them. This is because some info is out of context. For instance someone saying that they are being tortured by cupcakes is obviously not actual torture but you can still tag the person involved as a torturer. Having the discretion is nice but there are other times where you have to tag certain data to progress that I don’t feel was data that must have been tagged or as relevant as the game made it. I also don’t like how you can’t untag data. I also felt that at the end of the game there was supposed to be multiple ways to handle the outcome but I could only see one or possibly two. I don’t know why the other ways weren’t available to me as I can’t think of a story reason that I shouldn’t have been able to pull off what i wanted. The story was good but the twists near the end were simply fantastic. The UI for the game was easy to get used to and had a good design. I also liked how new parts of the software were revealed as they became needed. The game has no voice acting but that wasn’t an issue wand made sense given the fact that outside of recorded calls this was all  just you at a computer. The puzzle aspect was that you have to scour the various blogs; calls; emails; etc to find info you can use to further the game as well as provide additional depth details and context. 

	I played Orwell on Linux. It froze on me once but other than that I encountered no issues and noticed no spelling errors. There are no graphics options and the game has a 60 FPS cap. You can save on exit but there is just one save slot so you can’t undo choices or have multiple save files. Performance was good with no noticeable lag. Alt-Tab Didn’t work.

Graphics Engine: Unity
Graphics API: OpenGL
Game Version Played: 1.4.7479.33238
Disk Space Used: 639 MB

CPU Usage: 16-43 %
RAM Usage: 3.5-4.6 GB

	I enjoyed Orwell both for the way the game play was used as well as for the story and characters. I wish the ending had have been more open but as it was it’s still a great game. I finished it in four hours and 13 minutes and can say it is easily worth it’s current price tag of $11.49 CAD. 

My Score: 8/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

review_text_raw:
"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" seems content to repeat what books and movies have said more eloquently.  It also falls below the dollar per hour metric (it can be completed within 5 hours).

The gameplay is simple and involves clicking through fake internet websites, blogs, and chat logs to collect bits of information (a process that can easily become tedious).

So the appeal is obviously the story, but for $9.99, you're better off buying a copy of George Orwell's 1984, or Aldous Huxley's Brave New World instead. This game is nothing more than a shallow summary of the themes explored in depth by those literary works.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just finished my 1st playthrough, it took me about 5 hours or so.

I played in on Linux and it ran without any issue.

This is more of a Visual Novel than a game to me, so please be aware of that before being let down. There is no way to get stuck, the game always tells you what you need to click on, which is soso. There are a few choices at times, and there is also the option of not submitting some information to the system, that will alter the story somewhat.

I had a good time playing it, though at times I didn't really care about all the stuff I had to read... I still don't think I really needed to read all of it but I could be wrong. I wish there was some way to scale the text, as I play on a TV, sitting far from it. Unlike other games it's not too bad though. It feels like the whole thing should just have been in HTML/JS/CSS and allow easy scaling.

Alas, even though I started wondering about what happened and why and such, I never really cared about the characters. I find them unappealing in their own ways (mental problems, obnoxious people, etc). I never really got immersed in the story, never really felt part of it till people other than my boss start mentioning my character and by then it was too late to care.

As people have commented on the forum, even though I also assumed it was the goal, I never really got a bad feeling from the Orwell system, I think it kind of failed there, but maybe with another playthrough following some differents paths I'd feel different.

The idea of the novel and the way we play is interesting and different, that's definitely a plus, but that was pretty much all it had. Had it kept going on for 10 more episodes, I don't know if I would have finished it.

I got this game as it was suggested to me based on buying (and loving) Beholder. Between the 2 of them, I'd definitely suggest Beholder, though one is about technology not the other...

This review would a bit over neutral if I had the choice, but since I don't, it's thumbs up!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I usually don't like games with lots of reading. The exception to that rule is this game. The narrative being told from the view of the spy software Orwell with the player being the investigator using the tool, playing middleman between the AI and what actually gets processed, is a great twist to how visual novels usually work.

The game's interface, while relatively simple, but maybe a bit cluttered, is very easy to use while still giving the player tools to not get lost between sources of information, marking sources with new information, sources with unsubmitted "data chunks" and sources with disabled (marked by the player as not important or false information) "data chunks" with icons.

The artstyle is is unique and definitely detailed enough to get a good picture of the people involved in the story. The OST does its job very well and never got boring to me, even after multiple playthroughs, rare sound effects help convey the impact of situations very well.

Usually I only end up 100%ing games I like. I have long ago gotten 100% Achievements in this game and now just revisited it and enjoyed my latest playthrough.

The Linux version runs quite well but seems to have some graphical glitches at least on my system (intel i5-6600k, GTX970 with nvidia driver 435 on Kubuntu). Switching to the windows version using Steam Proton (I used gloriuseggroll's custom proton 5.4, but a user on protondb also had success with official proton 4.11) fixed these issues, while even keeping my save files, which is definitely a first.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is one of those games that makes you think. It makes you think about how surveillance works in the real world. It makes you think about what you put online as this can be misunderstood or taken out of context. It makes you think about what your credit card statement says about you. Most of all though it makes you think about what is considered as right and wrong.

Orwell is a game where you play a person sat at a computer terminal extracting information from the internet about people to stop a series of terrorist bombings. Through what information you decide to pass on to your handler and which conflicting statements you believe the game will pan out very differently. How relevant is it that somebody doesn’t like to go out and party? Not very much on the surface, but what if they later say they are going out clubbing all night? Seems unusual for somebody who actively dislikes this, doesn’t it? Are you reading too much into this? Or is this information going to stop a bombing? Orwell constantly asks you to reassess your understanding of the characters you are investigating. One phone call or chat message could convince you that they are a terrorist or vice versa and you need to just weather the consequences.

For the full review please visit [url]https://bitsandpieces.games/2017/03/02/orwell-review/[/url]
